{{Short description|Technique to find asymptotic expansions}}
In [[asymptotic analysis]], the '''method of Chester–Friedman–Ursell''' is a technique to find [[asymptotic expansion]]s for [[Contour integration|contour integrals]]. It was developed as an extension of the [[steepest descent method]] for getting uniform asymptotic expansions in the case of coalescing [[saddle point]]s.<ref>{{cite book|first1=Frank W. J.|last1=Olver|publisher=A K Peters/CRC Press|title=Asymptotics and Special Functions|date=1997|page=351|doi=10.1201/9781439864548|isbn=978-0-429-06461-6 }}</ref> The method was published in 1957 by [[Clive R. Chester]], [[Bernard Friedman (mathematician)|Bernard Friedman]] and [[Fritz Ursell]].<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Clive R.|last1=Chester|first2=Bernard|last2=Friedman|first3=Fritz|last3=Ursell|publisher=Cambridge University Press |title=An extension of the method of steepest descents |journal=[[Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society]] |volume=53 |number=3 |date=1957 |pages=599–611 |doi=10.1017/S0305004100032655}}</ref>

== Method ==
=== Setting ===
We study integrals of the form
:<math>I(\alpha,N):=\int_{C}e^{-Nf(\alpha,t)}g(\alpha,t)dt,</math>
where <math>C</math> is a contour and
* <math>f,g</math> are two analytic functions in the complex variable <math>t</math> and continuous in <math>\alpha</math>. 
* <math>N</math> is a large number.

Suppose we have two saddle points <math>t_+,t_-</math> of <math>f(\alpha,t)</math> with multiplicity <math>1</math> that depend on a parameter <math>\alpha</math>. If now an <math>\alpha_0</math> exists, such that both saddle points coalescent to a new saddle point <math>t_0</math> with multiplicity <math>2</math>, then the steepest descent method no longer gives uniform  asymptotic expansions.

=== Procedure ===
Suppose there are two simple saddle points <math>t_{-}:=t_{-}(\alpha)</math> and <math>t_{+}:=t_{+}(\alpha)</math> of <math>f</math> and suppose that they coalescent in the point <math>t_0:=t_0(\alpha_0)</math>.

We start with the ''cubic transformation'' <math>t\mapsto w</math> of <math>f(\alpha,t)</math>, this means we introduce a new complex variable <math>w</math> and write
:<math>f(\alpha,t)=\tfrac{1}{3}w^3-\eta(\alpha) w+A(\alpha),</math>
where the coefficients <math>\eta:=\eta(\alpha)</math> and <math>A:=A(\alpha)</math> will be determined later.

We have
:<math>\frac{dt}{dw}=\frac{w^2-\eta}{f_t(\alpha,t)},</math>
so the cubic transformation will be analytic and injective only if <math>dt/dw</math> and <math>dw/dt</math> are neither <math>0</math> nor <math>\infty</math>. Therefore <math>t=t_{-}</math> and <math>t=t_{+}</math> must correspond to the zeros of <math>w^2-\eta</math>, i.e. with <math>w_{+}:=\eta^{1/2}</math> and <math>w_{-}:=-\eta^{1/2}</math>. This gives the following system of equations 
:<math>\begin{cases}
f(\alpha,t_{-})=-\frac{2}{3}\eta^{3/2}+A,\\
f(\alpha,t_{+})=\frac{2}{3}\eta^{3/2}+A,
\end{cases}</math>
we have to solve to determine <math>\eta</math> and <math>A</math>. A theorem by Chester–Friedman–Ursell (see below) says now, that the cubic transform is analytic and injective in a local neighbourhood around the critical point <math>(\alpha_0,t_0)</math>.

After the transformation the integral becomes
:<math>I(\alpha,N)=e^{-NA}\int_L \exp\left(-N\left(\tfrac{1}{3}w^3-\eta w\right)\right)h(\alpha,w)dw,</math>
where <math>L</math> is the new contour for <math>w</math> and
:<math>h(\alpha,w):=g(\alpha,t)\frac{dt}{dw}=g(\alpha,t)\frac{w^2-\eta}{f_t(\alpha,t)}.</math>

The function <math>h(\alpha,w)</math> is analytic at <math>w_{+}(\alpha),w_{-}(\alpha)</math> for <math>\alpha\neq \alpha_0</math> and also at the coalescing point <math>w_0</math> for <math>\alpha_0</math>. Here ends the method and one can see the integral representation of the complex [[Airy function]].

Chester–Friedman–Ursell note to write <math>h(\alpha,w)</math> not as a single [[power series]] but instead as
:<math>h(\alpha,w)=\sum\limits_{m} q_m(\alpha)(w^2-\eta)^m+ \sum\limits_{m} p_m(\alpha) w(w^2-\eta)^m</math>
to really get asymptotic expansions.

=== Theorem by Chester–Friedman–Ursell ===
Let <math>t_{+}:=t_{+}(\alpha),t_{-}:=t_{-}(\alpha)</math> and <math>t_{0}:=t_{0}(\alpha_0)</math> be as above. The cubic transformation
:<math>f(t,\alpha)=\tfrac{1}{3}w^3-\eta(\alpha) w+A(\alpha)</math>
with the above derived values for <math>\eta(\alpha)</math> and <math>A(\alpha)</math>, such that <math>t=t_{\pm}</math> corresponds to <math>u=\pm\eta^{1/2}</math>, has only one branch point <math>w=w(\alpha,t)</math>, so that for all <math>\alpha</math> in a local neighborhood of <math>\alpha_0</math> the transformation is analytic and injective.
